subsubtopic: POLLUTION DANGER TO LAKE ONTARIO-MOTION UNDER S O. 43
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, a New York State study shows that levels of the deadly chemical dioxin in the Love Canal area during the years 1980 and 1981 were among the highest ever recorded. Just recently a United States district judge approved an environmentally unsound toxic waste agreement relating to the Hyde Park dump, one which will allow the continued seepage of deadly chemicals from the dump into the Niagara River and on into Lake Ontario. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe South (Mr. Stewart):
That whereas four million Canadians use the waters of Lake Ontario for drinking and recreational purposes, the Minister of the Environment take positive action now, even to the extent of taking legal proceedings so as to protect the water quality of Lake Ontario and particularly to prevent the agreement entered into with respect to the Hyde Park dump from becoming a precedent with respect to the Love Canal.

That the Prime Minister and his cabinet show Canadians how their 6 per cent restraint program will work and agree to lower their salaries to that of the ordinary Canadian, and that they attempt to feed, clothe and shelter their families on $18,600 this year, finding a way to cope with price increases that are currently running at twice the level of their recommended 6 per cent solution.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR REDUCTION IN INTEREST RATES-MOTION UNDER
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, despite attempts by the government, through measures contained in its recent budget and other hastily conceived responses, the situation with respect to the business community remains dangerously critical. In the first six months of this year business bankruptcies climbed to 5,383, that is, 37 per cent higher than during the same period last year. That is to say that 5,383 employers lost their businesses. Experts feel the number may be as much as five times higher when those who do not bother to file for bankruptcy are included in the total. The tragedy is compounded when, using estimates of 11 employees per company as an average, the number of jobs lost, because of these businesses folding, could be well over 250,000 since the first of the year. 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis):
That the government take immediate action to reduce high interest rates in Canada, rates 3 per cent higher than in the United States, and rates which are a direct, major cause of this devastation of our business community.

speechtext:

In May the New Democratic Party Environment Task Force released a report on the problems of toxic pollution in the Great Lakes and Niagara River. Since then there have been further reports of dioxin contamination, and further cutbacks to Great Lakes research by the Reagan administration. A task force recommendation for an all-party committee to study these and related problems was presented to this House by the NDP House leader on June 30. subsubtopic: INCREASE IN RATE OF GOVERNMENT REGULATED PRICES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. I am sure the minister is aware that a Statistics Canada paper has recently pointed out that while inflation increased during the period April, 1981, to April, 1982, by 11 per cent, government regulated prices, that is, prices on telephones and heating, and hidden taxes such as those on the sale of stamps and gasoline prices, have increased by 18 per cent, while market prices have increased by only 9 per cent. Since this government-controlled component of inflation has clearly played a predominant role in our inflationary problem, would the minister explain why the government has done nothing more than put a wishy-washy statement in his most recent budget to try to address this problem?

speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: INCREASE IN RATE OF GOVERNMENT REGULATED PRICES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the statement was clear and firm, and it will be implemented.

speechtext: When? 1986?

subsubtopic: INCREASE IN RATE OF GOVERNMENT REGULATED PRICES

Madam Speaker, the minister must surely be aware that regulatory bodies have to abide by legislation, by regulations, and by their past

Is the government proposing to issue a specific overriding statement to these bodies to put some teeth into the request he appears to have made and, if so, what will be the nature of such a directive?

In adition to that, it is the intention of the government to monitor very carefully all price changes within the government structure and to limit them to 6 per cent, unless circumstances justify different treatment.
What circumstances?

speechtext: This aspect of the 6 per cent limit will be followed very carefully by the government through the regulatory agencies and through the departments of government. If the hon. member has further suggestions as to how this particular aspect might be undertaken, I would be glad to hear from him because I expect he and his party would also be prepared to support all efforts to bring the economy from the present 12 per cent level of prices to a 6 per cent level of growth and recovery.

Madam Speaker, what I am trying to find out is whether there is something in the direction the minister is taking, or the whole government is taking, with respect to regulated prices which will have some teeth, which will work, and which will bring down regulated prices from the 18 per cent level of the past year to something closer to the 6 per cent and 5 per cent in the budget. Let me ask a final question of the minister. Since restraint efforts can only succeed if governments can be seen to be doing everything they can to control prices under their jurisdictions, and since prices are the main problem, would the minister

Madam Speaker, the hon. member has spoken about administered prices as if they were the single component of the restraint program. They certainly are an important component, but an even more important component is the wage restraint program which is now before the House of Commons. Wages and incomes constitute the greatest source of increases throughout the entire economy, the hon. member could help us all by getting the bill that is before the House to committee at the earliest possible date.
The hon. member will have to wait to see the program develop, because there will be specific instances of price increases that will be proposed in excess of 6 per cent that will have to be dealt with by the government. speechtext: Madam Speaker, may I address a question to the Minister of the Environment who is in charge of national parks. Given that restraint in increasing prices is essential if there is to be effective wage restraint; and given that this government is asking industry and business to keep down prices and wages; and given that in the Banff town site Parks Canada is holding wages to 6 per cent but is increasing rentals by from 15 to 40 per cent and perhaps more, is the government prepared to practise what it preaches and cut the proposed increases in land rents on August 1 to not more than 6 per cent?

speechtext:
To go into another area, Madam Speaker, we all know that the reason businesses, large, medium or small, are having difficulty surviving is because of high interest rates. The Bank of Canada Act, in Section 14(2) says:
-the Minister may. after consultation with the Governor and with the approval of the Governor in Council, give to the Governor a written directive concerning monetary policy, in specific terms and applicable for a specified period, and the Bank shall comply with such directive.
Is the Minister of Finance prepared to provide the survival mechanism for all business in Canada and all Canadians by directing the Governor of the Bank to lower interest rates?

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEachen (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance
subsubtopic: REQUEST THAT GOVERNOR BE DIRECTED TO LOWER INTEREST RATES
speechtext: Madam Speaker, the simplicity with which the hon. member asks the question might lead some people to believe that it is a solution to the current problems. There is no way in which an effective reduction of interest rates can take place without first a reduction in the level of interest rates in the U.S. and a reduction in the level of inflation in Canada. A directive to the Governor of the Bank seeking an arbitrary reduction in interest rates, unrelated to the economic facts which exist in the country, would have very damaging effects on the future of the economy. What might appear as a temporary lowering of interest rates would undoubtedly lead to a considerable number of adverse consequences, including subsequently higher interest rates in the country. That is why I have not thought it wise to ask the Governor in a directive to do the impossible.

Madam Speaker, the Government of Canada is very disappointed with the announcement of President Reagan that the United States will not participate in the Law of the Sea Treaty. We are presenting a note to the United Sates, I believe today, to that effect. Nevertheless, we will continue with our intention of making that treaty as universal as possible.
With respect to the kind of question that the hon. member asks, it is really far too soon to estimate the possible effects on employment. For example, the continued presence of the United States might have led to further modifications in the Law of the Sea Treaty with respect to deep seabed mining which might have been less favourable to Canada. I think it is therefore impossible for us to answer, in a precise and short fashion, the kind of question which he asks. The first one is Standing Order 60(8) which determines the procedure to be followed for putting the question on the budget motion, and it stipulates
July 14, 1982

very clearly that the Speaker shall interrupt the proceedings on the sixth day and forthwith put the question on the main motion. That is as clear as can be! This Standing Order should be read in conjunction with Standing Order 9(2) which deals with the time during which the bells may be sounded, and I quote:
When, under the provisions of any Standing Order or other order of this House, Mr. Speaker has interrupted any proceeding-
That was the case, since the proceedings had to be interrupted because of Standing Order 60(8).
-for the purpose of putting forthwith the question on any business then before the House, the bells to call in the Members shall be sounded for not more than fifteen minutes.
So this is very obvious, and the Standing Order is very clear in this respect. So much so, in fact, that, as I was told some time ago, the House Leader for the Progressive Conservative Party, the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) had taken steps to ensure that this Standing Order would be duly applied and that the bells would not be sounded for more than fifteen minutes. In fact, on that occasion his whip entered the House alone, and ours had to follow subsequently to allow the division to take place. These rules are not new, the procedure is known to everyone and the Standing Order is extremely straightforward.
Therefore, what is the member for Yukon's case against the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, who from his own seat, and in his own terms, was simply referring to established practice and to a Standing Order which is extremely clear in its wording? He was merely saying what the law prescribes and acting in accordance with parliamentary procedure and the Standing Orders. What is so reprehensible about all that? What is reprehensible, Madam Speaker, is the fact that on that evening, the Progressive Conservative members ignored parliamentary practice-as they ignored their own request on an earlier and similar occasion-and ignored the Standing Orders of the House. Today, in a very underhanded manner, and this is an understatement, Madam Speaker, they are trying to discredit an hon. member who was only seeking respect for this institution.
I want to congratulate the New Democratic Party House leader for his excellent judgment in the circumstances and for his courtesy in asking that the resignation, which in any case was not tendered according to form-it was not a real resignation-by the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell be reconsidered. He did not resign. I am happy to see that he acknowledges that this member is extremely valuable and that he has performed his duties well, both as the Chair's representative and from his seat in the House. However, I must deplore the less than direct and less than honest attitude shown by the Progressive Conservatives, who today are refusing to gave their consent, which is not absolutely essential, but they are refusing to acknowledge, out of courtesy, that the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell was only performing his role of experienced and responsible parliamentarian with a concern for the respect due Canada's Parliament. I deplore this attitude on their part, and as far as we are concerned, the member
Point of Order-Mr. Nielsen
for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell is experienced and responsible enough to make his own decisions. We welcome the support of the New Democratic Party, and once again, we deeply regret the lack of maturity, irresponsibility and childish attitude shown by the Progressive Conservatives and their leader.

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-RESIGNATION OF MR. ETHIER-POSITION OF OFFICIAL OPPOSITION
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I was involved in that the other night, as members know. After the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Ethier) had said what he had said, using the words applying to the members of my party that they are not acting as true representatives of this country, you recognized me, after you had asked the member to reconsider his decision. In just that previous statement-

And who happens to be the Deputy Speaker-

The matter being the charge that he made. That was the invitation put to the hon. member, in good faith. Then the hon. member said, in part:
I appreciate the kind words of the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton-I meant what I said before; I do not speak with a forked tongue, and I stand by what I said-if members do not live by the rules and procedures that were given to them by the Chair. Therefore, I stand by what I said a while ago. Please accept my resignation, Madam Speaker.
Now, Madam Speaker, I think that casts not only a burden on the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell but it casts a great burden on you because you have to decide whether or not that resignation, having been tendered and not withdrawn, ought to be accepted in these circumstances.
I regret to have to say this, because of what I said the other evening. I would think it would not serve the best interests of the House if the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell, not having accepted the invitation, which was put forward in good faith, to withdraw, at least to reconsider, at least to check, did not do so.
I say that with some considerable regret because I was one of those who at that time wanted that kind of withdrawal and went the second mile to try to achieve it.
If we are talking about peace in the House of Commons, it would be best if the member did not occupy the chair. I say that with great regret but I believe that as a member of the House of Commons I had best say it firmly, because I was involved the other evening.

speechtext:
1 hear a few little "ha, ha's" from the Tory caucus. Let me put my reasons four square. First of all, I can well appreciate the frustration and anger that was in the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell on that evening. I can well understand it, given that the reason for it was the fact that the members of the Conservative Party refused to come in for a vote and that there was no justification for their actions. Every other member in the House of Commons was being required to sit here and wait while they decided when and if the vote was going to be taken.
I put it quite bluntly that I resented it that evening, and I resent the unctuousness of the House leader of the official opposition when he rises and talks about people's responsibilities. It is about time he understood his responsibility.

Over the course of the last year we have had nothing but bullying bar-room tactics from the Tories. I am personally sick and tired of them.
On one evening they all rise en masse and walk out. And if 1 had not risen to oppose a request from the government for a House order they would have missed an opportunity to speak on a bill. On another day, they walk out of the House and refuse to come in and vote. On another day, they storm the Speaker's chair screaming and shouting like raving maniacs.
I say to you, Madam Speaker, that I seriously regret that the Conservative Party shows no generosity of spirit in this regard. I suggest to them that they should understand the duress under which the member was put and they should appreciate that he has, under normal conditions, acted fairly and impartially and that they should not take out their childish ignorance on that member.

subtopic: MR. NIELSEN-RESIGNATION OF MR. ETHIER-POSITION OF OFFICIAL OPPOSITION
speechtext:
May I interrupt the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) before he goes any further in this kind of exposition of the facts.
It is true that some information was asked for as to whether this was a 15- minute bell or not. Two persons were asked. Both answered, "Yes, it is a 15-minute bell". The second question was, "Could it go beyond 15 minutes?" The answer-more or less, but meaning the same thing-given by the two people in question was, "We have seen it go beyond," and that is an absolute fact; it often goes beyond 15 minutes. It does not go much beyond 15 minutes, but it does go beyond 15 minutes. That is the answer which was given, and it could only mean that it was a 15-minute bell but that it could possibly go beyond that time.
When l was told that there would be a delay in the vote, I said to a member of the Conservative caucus: "That is fine; I might wait for a while, but not indefinitely." I sent a message by one of the officers of the House to the Conservative caucus advising them that I would be taking the vote momentarily.
Those are the facts. I did have to rise, and I apologize if I had to interrupt the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition, a thing I do not like to do. However, as the Speaker I feel a very grave responsibility to defend the officers of the Table, who give advice privately to hon. members and to those who serve with me to the best of their knowledge.

As Your Honour has just indicated, the point has to do with the capacity of this House to accept the neutrality of the Chair. Our capacity to respect the neutrality of the Chair in the case of the hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Ethier) has been very seriously undermined by, first, the statements of that hon. member in the House, which have recently been read into the record of the House by the House leader of the official opposition. The hon. member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell said of Members of Parliament, whose servant he is and regarding whom he is supposed to act absolutely free of partisanship:
They are not acting as true representatives of this country.
July 14, 1982

Those were his words. He was subsequently immediately given an opportunity by the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) to study the facts, of which Your Honour has now apprised the House and the country. He cannot command our respect as someone who would carry out his responsibilities in a neutral way. That is the sum of the situation. He has had several days to repair his reputation. He has chosen not to exercise that option. We in this party can have no confidence in his neutral exercise of the functions of the Chair of the House of Commons.

I suppose a few words on my part in answer to the presentation made by the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) are in order at this point. If the hon. member reads carefully the words I spoke that evening, he will find I did not in any way accept the resignation of the Deputy Chairman of Committee of the Whole because, of course, the matter of resigning from the position he occupies is entirely between the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and himself.
I am perfectly aware that the hon. member was probably not well acquainted with exactly what was going on, and seeing that he was obviously quite disturbed by the fact that we might not be following the rules of the House as he understands them, he wanted to make a few remarks precisely about that matter. Knowing that he was not acquainted with the facts, hon. members will see, if they read Hansard, that I told him at that point that when he became acquainted with the facts, which I would be only too happy to explain to him later, he would probably want to reconsider what he was saying at that particular time.
As far as I am concerned, the hon. member is still serving the House in the capacity in which he has always enjoyed the confidence of the House until now. Unless there is a formal motion to the contrary, I cannot allow the conduct of an hon. member to be discussed further. The only way to discuss the conduct of an hon. member, of course, is by a formal motion to that effect. As far as I am concerned, the hon. member still has the confidence of the House.
1 leave it entirely to him to decide whether he wants to clarify some of the statements he made on that particular evening. He may do that. The hon. member has taken a few days of rest. I think he was particularly disturbed at the events that evening, so he has taken a few days of rest-

Madam Speaker, I agree that you have no onus here with respect to the matter. The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Mackasey) was correct as far as he went, when he said that the only person who has the power to consider the resignation is the person who appointed the hon. member. That is the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). He may or may not want to take action on the strength of the words that the hon. member used that evening.
I would point out that neither is the onus on this party to take any steps. There was a clear, repeated statement by the hon. member that evening that he was resigning. On the first occasion the statement was directed to the Prime Minister and members of his caucus. He made the second statement, in the event that it was not quite clear to whom the resignation should be submitted, to you while you were in the chair. On two occasions he stated quite clearly that he was resigning. I therefore agree that there is no onus on the Chair for the reasons stated and there is certainly no onus here. We are acting, in future, on the strength of that resignation.

subsubtopic: MR. SHIELDS-AIRCRAFT PARKING FEES AT FORT McMURRAY AIRPORT
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have the responsibility and the duty to present a petition on behalf of a number of my constituents in the riding of Athabasca. The purpose of the petition, signed by 46 residents of Fort McMur-ray, who are private pilots and aircraft owners, is to register their protest against the decision taken by the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin) to charge aircraft parking fees at the airport in Fort McMurray.
The nature of this petition is to request that the government immediately withdraw this parking fee until such time as the parking lot at the Fort McMurray airport is upgraded to a level deserving of a parking charge. The parking area is nothing more than a gravel pit which cost nothing to build and costs nothing to maintain. The petitioners request that Transport Canada improve the quality and safety of the parking lot at the Fort McMurray airport before the charging of parking fees is considered.
The petitioners hope, in Madam Speaker's examination of this petition, that you will find the petition is in order, sense the urgency of their plea, and that you might use the discretionary powers vested in your office to allow discussion and referral of this petition to the Standing Committee on Transport at the earliest possible moment.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, in my comments on Bill C-124 last night I had begun to show how certain of the assumptions the Liberals have made in their economic strategy are seriously flawed. I would like to continue that critique by examining the Liberal theory of inflation and the way this bill shows that they either do not understand inflation or they refuse to acknowledge the real causes because doing so would involve much more courageous decisions than simply blaming the average Canadian.
Liberal views of inflation do not seem to take into account the tremendous increases in energy costs which have taken place since 1973, and particularly the last few years. Those increases have cut into the viability of the economy as it had been previously organized. The needed transition from a cheap energy economy to an expensive one will require more than simply asking average Canadians to take less so that the wealthy and powerful can maintain the standard of living to which they have become accustomed. The reality of a shrinking economic pie means that those who have much will have to take less in order that those who do not have so much will be able to maintain what they have. Anything other than this approach means a departure from what Canadians have come to believe about the Canadian commitment to greater equality of the human condition. Yet it is precisely the opposite approach that the Liberals have taken by giving in to the demand of the powerful that their standard of living be protected at all costs, even if it means cutting back on things like pensions.
However, Mr. Speaker, related to the problem of increased energy costs is the whole issue of diminishing returns on capital investment. Capital invested in energy extraction is increasingly unproductive and burdensome. For example, witness the situation of Dome Petroleum which is in trouble in spite of the fact that for years it has received over a dollar from the Canadian public for every dollar it spent on exploration. Witness the malaise of the debt-ridden nuclear industry in this and other countries. Those are two good examples of the increasing unviability of traditional energy extraction projects, but it is not only in that area that the traditional notions of capital investment are breaking down. It is happening in many other sectors as well. Productivity needs to be seen not just as labour productivity. There is also the question of the declining productivity of capital investments. The productivity of traditional investment models has been overrated for years. In
19332

July 14, 1982
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
fact, it has been assumed that the only productivity that ever needed to be improved was labour productivity. In reality, the success of capital investment strategies in the past has relied on the ability of the private sector to externalize the social and environmental costs of their decisions, to pass on those costs to consumers, taxpayers and governments. Governments then ring up large deficits in coping with these externalized costs, and they are then reviled by the same private sector for overspending.
The fact of the matter is, Mr. Speaker, that these externalized bills of the economic system under which we have lived for far too long are coming due. Rather than face up to this, the Liberals are trying to put off the evil day. They cannot show leadership on this issue. Their ties to the people whose self-interest and ideological assumptions need to be challenged are too close. Indeed, they are often the same people. We all know of the great incestuous relationship which exists between the boardrooms of the nation and the Liberal caucus and former cabinet ministers. Meanwhile, of course, the Conservatives are still fantasizing about a return to the heyday of the kind of economy which brought us to where we are now. In this respect they are philosophically useless and, practically speaking, very dangerous in the kind of ideas they are trying to promote. Mr. Speaker, there will be no turning back of the clock. President Reagan and the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Clark) are wrong.

speechtext: Everyone is wrong except you.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext: I for one would not like to see the clock turned back even if it could be, if by that we mean a return to the heyday of capitalism and the further destruction of the community, the environment and the future that that would involve.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext: It built everything this country has.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
The only way out of our present situation is to go ahead. This will require a critical approach to all of our assumptions-I mean by everyone-about how the modern economy works. In my view there appear to be at least two very different problems we have to face. The first is to a degree contained within the system as it now operates, that is, the increasing extent to which the western economies are now being victimized by the global mobility of the very corporations that use them to develop into the very powerful institutions that they now are. I touched a bit on this in my speech last night. Domestic and international justice is what is at stake in this question. This raises the age-old question of removing macroeconomic decision-making from the confines of private self-interested boardrooms, and bringing our economy under public control so that the common good will be the criterion for investment decisions and for technological decisions, not the profit margins of the global corporations.
The second problem, Mr. Speaker, is that of the economic model within which all of us too often work, whether of the left or the right. That is the model which assumes infinite growth in a finite world. It sees increasing economic growth in the traditional sense as the solution to all our problems. As we face
the deindustrialization of Canada as a result of multinational decisions, and as we face the increasing counterproductivity of traditional energy strategies and other capital-intensive strategies, we must look to how we might reindustrialize our economy, you might say, to fit the new global realities. Hopefully we will be able to do this in a global context free from the distorting and destructive decisions of the global corporations. That would make the transition much easier because they will resist us, they will try to accommodate the world economy to these new realities in a way which serves their interest and which will make what is needed much more difficult.
Some speak of what is coming as the post-industrial age. Others might prefer to call it reindustrialization. But whatever we call it, it will have to be done deliberately and intelligently. The invisible hand of Adam Smith, in which my colleagues on the right still fervently believe, will not lead us out of the mess we are in. Indeed, it has led us to the mess we are in. The invisible hand of Adam Smith is more like an invisible foot which tramples clumsily and insensitively on social, human and environmental needs rather than responds to these needs, as my friends to the right would dearly love to believe.
Neither, of course, will publicly planned economies dependent upon the wrong assumption and on the wrong goals lead us out of the mess we are in. We all need to move out of the era of large, top-heavy bureaucratic organizations, public or private, which maximize material production and wasteful consumption based on non-renewable resources and into the era of economies based on regenerative resources and energy, managed for sustained yield productivity, that is, the sustainable society. That is the era in which we should move now if we are to show any leadership at all here in this House.
We can have an exciting future if we would just let go of some of our traditional assumptions about the economy, about what constitutes economic growth and about what constitutes a standard of living. If we let go of those assumptions and acted with an imagination tempered by justice and the vision of a renewed human community in which people are no longer commodities but real people whose dignity and whose potential are irreplaceable, our future would be bright.
I believe that the philosophical and the political tradition which the New Democratic Party represents has the conceptual resources to deal with these problems. If I did not think that, I would not be standing here today. We cannot change in this country or in any other country what we do not control, what we cannot have any say in. And it is only the New Democratic Party in this country which is committed to bringing important economic decisions before the bar of the common good, however we may come to define that in the years ahead.
There is another cause of inflation, very seldom mentioned in this House, which needs to be mentioned. It is the point I have been trying to make all along. It is far too simplistic and
July 14, 1982

it is like hiding your head in the sand to imagine that wages are the cause of inflation in the western economies. Another cause of inflation is the arms race. That is only too seldom mentioned. The hundreds of billions of dollars which are spent on the arms race create deficits, distort spending priorities of governments all around the world and perpetuate underdevelopment in Third World countries.
Here is another area where the Liberals have talked a big show about disarmament, but wimped out when it came down to the wire. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) went to the Special Session on Disarmament at the United Nations, he did not say anything significant at all. Anybody could have said what the Prime Minister said. He showed no leadership. He showed no independence from American foreign policy. What he said was just the same old following along. Now that it is not what Alexander Haig says, I guess it will be what Mr. Shultz says. Whatever he says will guide what the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacGuigan) has to say.
The Conservatives, of course, have not bothered to pretend that they are for arms reduction. All they do is to try to exploit the peace movement for political purposes by branding disarmament people as Soviet sympathizers, and thus doing what harm they can to an important cause, just like when they side with murderous regimes in central and South America.
The world is in the grip of powerful, irresponsible forces that must be challenged. Here in Canada, under the leadership of the Liberal Party, we can either become the banana republic that we have in a way always been, or we can begin to build anew our own house. We can get our own house in order, and from there be able to contribute to a more just and sustainable global society. The Liberals and Conservatives will not acknowledge this reality. We do acknowledge it. We invite all Canadians who love life, who love freedom and the notion of a renewed human community to join with us. We do not have all the answers, but we have the political freedom which the two other parties have demonstrated time and time again they do not have. We have the political freedom to begin the work that needs to be done.
1 want to say something about the Progressive Conservative response to Bill C-124. It is hard to know just what the Progressive Conservative response to Bill C-124 is. When the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) rose, he sort of weaseled and waffled his way and was not sure just what the position of his party was with regard to this bill. Do you know what the problem is, Mr. Speaker? Right now, the Conservatives would vote against anything that was proposed by the Liberals and for anything that is in opposition to the Liberals. I need only refer to recent motions where the Conservatives voted for the strengthening of FIRA, and then, on the next day, someone in the Progressive Conservative Party moved a motion under the provisions of Standing Order 43 calling for the weakening of the Foreign Investment Review Agency. They did not even have the decency to wait 48 hours. The Progressive Conservatives voted for a tax on excess bank profits. I am sure that if we moved a motion calling for the
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
nationalization of the banking community in this country, the Tories would vote for it because they are so desperate to create the impression that they are different from the guys over there. They are not any different from the guys over there. But that is what is going on. The Tories will vote for anything. Now they do not know what to do on this bill. They have a real dilemma on their hands. The Progressive Conservatives approve of this program. They approve of Bill C-124. This program does not go as far as the hon. member for York-Peel (Mr. Stevens) would have liked to have led his party when it was in power, but it is getting there. It is called, "Blame the public sector. Blame the civil servant. Blame government spending." It is the sort of simplistic economic analysis that we always hear the members of the Conservative Party mouthing incessantly until we are almost sick to our stomachs from having to listen to it.
The Conservatives really want to vote for this bill, but they have to create the impression that they are different from the Liberals. It will be interesting to see what they will do. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) has now given notice of closure. The day of decision for the Progressive Conservative caucus is nigh. We wait with some anticipation just to see how far the Conservative Party has strayed into that area of politics where they vote for things purely on strategic considerations that have nothing to do with politics or have nothing to do with what they actually believe is the case. The irony of it is that every day the Conservatives become more and more like the Liberal Party.
Of course, they started out like two peas in a pod. But, in a more generous moment, we used to be able to say that the Progressive Conservatives had a few principles. They were dumb principles, but they had a few principles on which they liked to stand in relation to the Liberals. But that is not the case any more. Now the Conservatives will vote for anything. That is what happens when it comes to Bill C-124 and other matters.

Let one thing be clear, that from the analysis of the situation which I have attempted to lay out this afternoon and last night, the Liberals and the Conservatives are of a piece. When it comes down to the Liberals making a choice between protecting the people of this country and protecting their sources of campaign funds and sources of power, or when it comes down to choosing between the people of this country and the big money, the big money wins. There are only two ways the government can go. It can accept some responsibility and live up to its actions, or else this system, this institution, will have to be reformed. Again, we would have to look at the examples in other countries. We have to restore the power to the people themselves. People can no longer trust the ones they elect to Parliament. If they can no longer trust their government to be accountable, to be honest, to be sincere, to be less devious than this government, then we must change the system and restore to the people the powers that there are in other systems. 1 make the comparison to the system in the United States. The ordinary American can impeach his president. He can, in fact, recall his congressman or senator. Can one imagine how many Canadians would like to recall their Minister of Finance and replace him with someone else? Americans can elect their judges. They can present petitions to deny spending power to their governments. Proposition 13 was an example. We cannot have it both ways. This is the second reading of Bill C-124. It is an opportunity to examine the various principles involved in the legislation before the House. I was disappointed when the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) stood in the House earlier today and said that not only was the government going to remove the right to bargain collectively on the part of employees in the public service, but that he was going to eliminate one of the most fundamental and democratic rights this House has come to enjoy, freedom of debate, particularly on a very critical issue.
Bill C-124 is one of the most critical bills to come before this House in months. The fact that the government is going to introduce closure so that members will not have an opportunity to thoroughly debate the implications of this legislation is very disappointing.
This bill to restrict the wages and salaries of federal employees to 6 per cent in the first year and 5 per cent in the second year is a response of the government to the economic crisis facing Canada today. It was detailed precisely and extensively by past and present auditors general when they said that this country was on the edge of economic and financial collapse. I am sure every member of this House, both on the government side and the opposition side, will agree with that evaluation of our present economic situation. Indeed we are on the edge of financial and economic collapse.
It is also a response, Mr. Speaker, of the government to the wrestling match of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) with inflation. He is spending a lot of time on the battlefield wrestling inflation to the ground. He is not a successful fighter in that respect. It is proposed that Bill C-124 will assist us in our efforts to reduce the rate of inflation.
I do not have to remind members that we are in a situation where practically two million Canadians are forced into a state of idleness. We are becoming more familiar every day with what that state of idleness does to people. We know the depression, the distress, the anxiety, the lowering of morale that will have profound consequences for decades to come.
I say that, Mr. Speaker, because when you have so many people unemployed in a country, it has a ripple effect that can be measured in a variety of social terms. By social terms I refer to family breakups, family violence, drug abuse, alcohol abuse, increased juvenile delinquency. Youngsters are having trouble at school as a result of the financial problems their parents have to face. Again, the cost of these social problems will be with us, not for years but for decades and perhaps for even a generation or two.

We find out today that bankruptcies in the first half of 1982 have increased 37 per cent over last year, which we all know were at excessively high levels. We hear that plants across the country are operating at less than 70 per cent capacity. This 70 per cent capacity results directly in increased shutdowns, increased cutbacks, employee hiring freezes, lay-offs and the threat of future lay-offs. Growing numbers of Canadians are finding themselves dependent now on UIC benefits or welfare benefits. I am sad to have to say, Mr. Speaker, that in my constituency-which is one of the richest parts of the province of British Columbia, which is one of the richest parts of Canada, which is one of the richest countries in the world-the greatest contributor to the local economy is the UIC office today. When a Member of Parliament has been forced, because of people who fall between the cracks of UIC benefits and welfare benefits, to open a food bank to assist families who are unable to put food on the table for their families, it is a very sad comment on the state of our economic affairs.
As these plants close down, cut back, or lay off their employees, and as those people who are unemployed are unable to purchase goods and services, those who are fortunate to be working today are hesitant to purchase goods and services, because they are uncertain about their future. Six months from now, where is Canada going to be? It is certainly anything but clear, Mr. Speaker. As a result, the purchasing power of Canadians has been throttled.
Then the government comes along in its budget of June 28 with an idea. They say: "Because our plants are operating at undercapacity, because people are not able to purchase the durable goods that they desire and need, or the services they desire and need, we have a solution; we are going to cut back even further, we are going to reduce wages, we will increase taxation, we will relatively cut the pensions of the people who built this country." The logic of that argument escapes me. At a time when the economy is downturning because firms cannot sell their commodities or their services, the solution is to cut back on those sales even further. That logic, as I say, escapes me.
During these times of economic crisis and economic calamity, where businesses, small, medium or large, are struggling to survive, the government has looked about for a scapegoat, for a whipping boy, for a bogyman. "We have to blame someone; we cannot blame ourselves, we have to blame someone else." So they did some polling. We are used in this country to government policy by polling, so presumably using the services of Goldfarb or Gallup, they found that the public perception of a villain focused on federal employees, considered to be lazy, overpaid. Therefore, the government decided to introduce legislation to assist the Prime Minister in his battle of wrestling inflation to the ground by limiting the wage and salary increases of federal employees to 6 per cent and 5 per cent.
The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) stand up in this House daily and say: "This will wrestle inflation to the ground; this will reduce inflation." The Minister of Finance reminds me of Peter Pan. Peter Pan said that if you really believe you can fly, you will fly. The minister says that if you really believe this will reduce inflation, it will reduce inflation.
We on this side do not believe in Peter Pan. We do not believe this is the appropriate policy to reduce inflation or to resolve the economic challenges that face Canada today. How can we have confidence in the minister's inflation-fighting device when we find that energy increases for next year will exist at the 31 per cent level? By government policy, the energy prices in Canada will increase 31 per cent next year. As a result of the ripple effect of that, there will be an increase in transportation costs, in heating costs, in cooling costs. These are going to result, of course, in fuelling the rate of inflation.
What about the $135 billion accumulated deficit that by definition will drive the interest rates even higher than they are today? Mark my words. How can you keep inflation down when you have interest rates in the 21, 22, 23 percentile range? Again, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that by definition it is impossible. Yet somehow, mysteriously, by restricting the wages of 5 per cent of working Canadians, we will have this magical impact of reducing the rate of inflation down to the 6 per cent and 5 per cent world. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of Finance exists in a fairyland, that this world of 6 per cent and 5 per cent cannot exist under present government policies.
Why should we ask Canadians to follow along these guidelines voluntarily, in the absence of any over-all strategy or comprehensive program to fight inflation? As a result, we have many individuals, many groups of people, who are scrambling today in fear of their jobs or their futures. They are grabbing whatever they can in this desperate world that the government has created. You cannot blame people often for what we would tend to call being greedy, for asking for too much when the future is so uncertain for the workers of this country. Unlike the workers of Japan, which often the Prime Minister and Minister of Finance hold up as an example, where there is job security in those small, medium and large firms, where people do not have to scramble for their lives in this sort of free enterprise world in which we live.

I do not think that has changed much to this present day, when the reference earlier was to Dome Petroleum. We know full well that the taxpayers of Canada, when the crunch comes, will be called in to bail out that "free enterprise" firm because of imprudent decision-making on its

People in one category of the federal public service will get $6,000 increases and the majority of those in another bracket will receive increases in the $700 range. Anyone who calls that fair is a dreamer and believes in unicorns.

speechtext:
It is a sad day for Canada when we are debating- now under the cloud of closure-a bill which treats the employees of any institution so unfairly and then ask Canadians to rally around this "wonderful" program. That really is asking too much.
Many comments have been made over the last number of days that this bill is necessary in order to improve the competitiveness of Canada in international markets. Editorialists are prone to say that the wages of Canadians are so high that we are now unable to compete in the international marketplace. I want to consider that for a moment or two. The Majority of our exports are not labour-intensive at all. I refer, of course, to our huge wheat sales, huge energy sales and coal sales. These are major export commodities which are not labour-intensive. The wages of employees in these sectors play a relatively small part in the over-all expense, particularly during these times of high interest rates.
Let us look at the manufacturing sector. We hear cries that we cannot manufacture in this country because our wages are too high. Let us examine the facts and then decide. I will refer to manufacturing wage rates in a variety of countries which trade with one another. These wage rates were applicable in the year 1980. 1 choose that year not because of any selectiveness but because that is the year for which we have the most accurate data. The average manufacturing wage rate in Belgium, a major trading partner of Canada, was $13.18 per hour; in Sweden it was $12.60 per hour; in The Netherlands, $12.18 per hour; in West Germany, $11.94 per hour; in the United States of America, $9.92 per hour; in France, $9.46 per hour; and in Canada, $9.06 per hour. We ranked seventh among those countries, which are some of our major trading partners.
Over the last few years in West Germany, for example, which is one of our major trading partners, since 1975 manufacturing wages have increased by 91 per cent; in the United States by 56 per cent and in Canada by 48 per cent.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext: Why do you not talk about productivity at the same time?

speechtext: I could discuss productivity at some length, Mr. Speaker.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING COMPENSATION IN THE PUBLIC SECTOR OF CANADA
speechtext:
I feel it is appropriate to be relevant in our speeches, unlike some other hon. members whose comments were totally irrelevant.
When we consider productivity, do we consider the individual worker or the fact that in Canada we have branch plants which were never intended to be competitive on the international market in most cases? I do not think that matter is appropriate to a debate on wage and salary limitations for federal employees. I believe in the rule of relevancy, Mr. Speaker.
I have tried to indicate that wages in the manufacturing sector of this country relate relatively well to those of other
trading nations. When we speak of competition, does that mean that we want to compete with the multinational companies that choose their plant locations in order to take advantage of the cheapest labour possible-virtually slave labour? 1 have visited many plants in Third World countries where conditions could only be described as virtual slavery, where wages are 25 cents per hour. Do we want to participate in that kind of blind reaction that causes the difficulty in which we find ourselves today.
To what extent are federal employees the major cause of inflation? An interesting picture emerges from an examination of the increases in their wages over the past few years. In 1978 wage increases for federal employees averaged 6.6 per cent while for the same year inflation was 8.8 per cent; in 1980 wage increases for federal employees averaged 6.6 per cent and inflation was 9.4 per cent; in 1981 wage increases for federal employees averaged 8.8 per cent in the first quarter and the inflation rate was 12.2 per cent. These wage settlements were two to four points under the rate of inflation.
Are the real causes of inflation in this country employee wages in the private or public sector, or are they the result of government pricing through regulatory agencies as announced earlier today, when we found out that in past years the prices that the government could control increased by an average of 18 per cent? This covers energy prices and high interest rates. Surely those are the critical causes of inflation, not wage settlements of federal employees that range from two to four points below the average rate of inflation.
Who has most strongly advocated wage controls, Mr. Speaker? Who appeared not long ago in Ottawa saying that the answer to our problems was to control incomes? Let me read from a list of a few of the people who were advocating that reduction of wages was the obvious step to take. These people would obviously have a real sensitivity to the strains and stresses felt by the breadwinners in the country today, those people who are trying to make their mortgage payments and put food on the table. There was Mr. Ed Phillips, Chairman of Westcoast Transmission, whose income in 1980-81 increased from $257,656 to 444,836; David Culver, president of Alcan, whose income increased in 1981 from $392,601 to $447,702; the chairman of Bell Canada had a tough time in 1981 when his income increased from $514,000 to $626,000. Then there was the chairman of Seagram's Mr. Bronfman, whose income increased in 1981 from $887,646 to over $1 million. If his increase had been limited to 6 per cent he would have received only a $63,000 increase in that year. These are the people who are advocating wage controls as the answer to the country's problems. The government's credibility evaporates when one sees the people who are advising it-other than the polls-regarding this program.
In spite of the advice given by leaders of industry and business regarding wage controls-and that is not a surprise-
suggest that if the truth were known the wisest business leaders in the country would not advocate wage controls
July 14, 1982

because they recognize the long-term results that flow from them. We remember what happened a few years ago when the Anti-Inflation Board attempted to wrestle inflation to the ground. Most members will recall the period from 1975 to 1978. We were not dealing then with 5 per cent of the work force but with wage guidelines for all Canadians. I remember that a number of my acquaintances were scoffing and laughing because while everyone else's wages were restricted, they were finding new positions and their wages were going up; they were manipulating new jobs that were created for them and they were being hired back and forth by various firms. In other words, there was always a way around the regulations.
In 1975 the rate of inflation was 10.6 per cent. The target for the anti-inflation program was to reduce it to 8 per cent in 1976, 6 per cent in 1977 and 4 per cent in 1978. But when the program terminated in 1978 the rate of inflation was 9 per cent. And at what a price! The business and industrial leaders of the country know the reality of the situation. They know that the price was the thousands and thousands of Canadians who lost their jobs and as a result could not contribute in any way to the economy. That was the price of a one percentage point reduction in the rate of inflation, as well as the incredible bureaucracy that was built up and which laid a dark shroud over the country for three years.
There is one insidious aspect of this legislation that I do not like to talk about because I really cannot believe it is happening in Canada. This is a country that prides itself on being free, on providing opportunities for people, on freedom of speech, freedom of assembly and freedom of religion. We have just spent two years discussing the Charter of Rights. In the next breath, however, the government introduces a bill to remove free collective bargaining from public employees. The member opposite says "Oh, come on". That is what this bill does, if she reads it. It eliminates free collective bargaining. Set aside for the moment the question of the right to strike, which some members might want to argue about at some other point. We are talking about free collective bargaining. We are talking about a House which stood up day after day in support of the Solidarity movement in Poland, saying that this was a basic human right which any person should have. This government has removed that freedom from its own employees for the next two years, of course thereby breaking its contracts.
Free collective bargaining is an integral part of any free and democratic society. This bill denies federal employees the right to negotiate any items, including monetary items. The monetary items are set by guidelines, and the ability to negotiate such areas as flexible working hours, work sharing and technological change provisions, occupational health and safety provisions, security against unfair disciplinary action, maternity or parental leave, affirmative action, equal pay for equal work-

Mr. Speaker, this bill denies the right of nearly
500,000	employees to negotiate in those very critical areas during these presumably enlightened 1980s. To make Canada work, the government has decided to remove the basic democratic rights that the people have come to enjoy after a long and difficult struggle.
Let us be honest about the basis of many of our problems. I know we on this side are prone to hurl barbs across the way at the incompetence demonstrated by the federal government. That is our job, to criticize the federal government and the legislation it introduces. But there is another problem in our country and it has to do with the business of strikes. We have seen a very special strike occur in the last number of months in our land. It is not the kind of strike that normally riles some Canadians; it is a strike of capital. It really began with the first discussions about the National Energy Program. It was a decision by capital, domestic and foreign, to bring the economy to its knees. The Americans made no bones about it. They said they wanted to bring their cash home, and they did not hesitate despite knowing that it would destroy the economies of a variety of countries.
Capital went on strike in Canada as well. It is a sad day, Mr. Speaker, when on a daily basis we hear many business leaders standing up and criticizing this government for its inaction when in fact the strike of capital, in a not so subtle way, has equally resulted in the downturn of our economy over the last number of months. As a result of our economic structure, Canada has, because of a national policy, found itself to be a branch plant economy of countries like the United States.
My friends to the right, Mr. Speaker, the Progressive Conservatives, talk on and on about the free enterprise world in which we live. It was Sir John A. Macdonald who introduced the protective policies which enabled the manufacturing industries of Central Canada to be protected to a certain extent and use domestic resources to fuel their plants. That is not free enterprise in any way, shape or form. Today we have the same situation where the decisions about our future, whether to invest or grow in this or that particular area, whether to support and develop this or that kind of agriculture or other resources, are being made in boardrooms in the United States, Japan, Germany, the United Kingdom and other countries.
Therefore, it amazes me when the Progressive Conservatives stand up daily and say the answer to our problem is to remove FIRA and encourage more foreign decision-making regarding our future, and more foreign investment. They are saying the problem is also the solution, and I must say the logic escapes me.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that we are facing very difficult economic times. Many would say we are on the verge of a full-scale depression. I want to make it clear that we in the New Democratic Party feel that the way to stop this recessionary trend and initiate economic recovery is not by restricting the wages and salaries of federal employees.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very glad to have an opportunity to speak against Bill C-124 because I think it is quite possibly a watershed in legislation. I think this is a special occasion and it makes some of us, at least, think back about 37 years. This legislation may very well mark the end of an era. Those of us who remember World War II and being demobilized in 1945 can remember the sense of hope we had. We can remember the great excitement about the sort of new world we were facing. There was a great vision of what we were going to do after the war. We had defeated fascism, so we thought. There was a great deal of enthusiasm all over the world for reconstruction of those countries which had been damaged in the war, and those countries constricted by war production had great opportunities for expansion into new kinds of peacetime construction and development. There was a hunger for reconstruction and growth. It was that new vision, enthusiasm and hopeful expectation which was the basis for the kind of social peace and co-operation which has lasted for perhaps three decades.
The watchword, as I and others will recall, when we came out of the forces in 1945 was: full employment. We all remember that the unemployment of the thirties was only six years previous. The one thing that everyone, parties of the left, right and centre, political and labour movements of all kinds, agreed on was full employment. There was no need to force people to be idle while production goes down and people are in want. That was the basis of a kind of social contract 37 years ago. But this legislation now before us signals that the government has cancelled that understanding with the Canadian people. This legislation breaks that social contract.
It is not the first sign of the breaking. There have been many other things which I will not detail now, but this is an open wound. It is even more severe than the action of 1975. At the beginning it affects only half a million or perhaps a million workers, depending upon how many in the private sector may be on contract with the government. But we have the warning of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) that there may very well be more to follow.
What has been done by the Prime Minister and by the Liberal caucus with the full approval of the leader and members of the Tory caucus is to break that social contract made at the end of the war in 1945 and to introduce a kind of naked class legislation, harsher than I think we have seen in the last 37 years. We would probably have to go back to iron heel Bennett or to Borden's class legislation of 60 or more years ago to find the like of it.
This is class legislation against employees. Employees are specifically singled out for discriminatory treatment. Discrimination will be applied against them because they are employees. Employees are now second-class citizens in Canada. We had a signal of this. The Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) signalled this in the opening remarks of his budget on November 12, 1981. He said that "excessive income demands on the part of those employed denies employment to others." There is no mention of excessive demands on the part of employers and investors, those who buy the labour of others.
Only those who are forced to sell their labour are accused of being the cause of the unemployment of their fellow workers.
In this legislation we have exactly the same principle. Apparently there are some members across the way who do not believe that collective bargaining has been destroyed for at least two years. I presume they just rely on the caucus to tell them which way to vote and so have not found it necessary to read Bill C-124. When they do get around to Bill C-124, they will find Clause 7 which reads:
Every collective agreement or arbitral award that includes a compensation plan that is extended under section 4 or 5 shall, subject to this Part, continue in force without change for the period for which the compensation plan is extended.
In other words, a whole union contract is frozen, extended for two years. Employees are not allowed to bargain even on non-monetary items. That is the clear reading of those words. That is how that clause is read by hundreds of thousands or millions of people in this land, probably everyone here except the people sitting in the backbenches across the way.
That is class legislation by people who preach unity and cooperation, the co-operation of the horse and the rider. This government has destroyed what has been won through a century or a century and a half of negotiation, namely the recognition of the right to collective bargaining. This government cannot destroy the right to collective bargaining. That is inherent to basic relationships and to basic humanity of the men and women of this country and other countries of the world. What is being destroyed is the government's recognition of that right. The Liberals are inviting the severest kind of social disorder in this country by doing that.
There is no legislation whatever touching on a limitation of profits. There is no legislation whatever touching on a limitation of prices. The class of investors and employers gets off scot-free and is the beneficiary of this wage freeze legislation.
It is ironic to listen to some of the Tories warning of the social unrest that will come from this. They have admitted that they will be voting with the Liberals for this class legislation. It is not surprising. For once the Tories have been uncharacteristically consistent. Their former leader, Mr. Stanfield, first preached the idea of this class legislation. But in case there was any doubt, their leader, the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark), said on July 5: "What is in this budget? There is one important initiative: the introduction of restraint on public sector salaries." Since then a number of his followers have joined him in supporting that statement.
The Tories like to rail against us any time we vote with the government, but on this most important piece of legislation, the most important for several years, the Tories will do all they can to support it. As one hon. member said yesterday, the Tories will get on the 6 per cent and 5 per cent bandwagon. The Tories will climb on the bandwagon that has been created by the people with whom they pretend to disagree.
This new budget is an attack on the working people of Canada. It is a worse budget than the budget of November, 1981. This budget adds to the attack made then. This budget
July 14, 1982

cuts the wages of the employee. That is to say, it cuts them clearly below what the government predicts is the cost of living. This budget cuts and will cut benefits to the unemployed. Cuts have been made administratively. Already the government is reducing staff in the unemployment and pension offices. The government will simply drag out the process of applications.
Soon the government will put an extra tax on those workers still working in order to pay for the cover-up schemes which the government has, like the cover-up scheme when you take four jobs and stretch those jobs among five people, claiming you have created a job. The government will be cutting benefits to the unemployed and it will be cutting welfare payments further than has already been done. Welfare is all there is left for somebody who has been left out of unemployment insurance benefits or who has run through his unemployment insurance benefits.
In its haste to introduce naked class legislation, the government has shown complete contempt for contracts. The government has signed contracts with its employees. The government urges employees to bargain in good faith. The government sets the laws of bargaining in good faith and then the government wipes them out. It is not the first time the government has done this. The government previously granted the right to strike, but when that right was used the government cancelled it.
There are two kinds of laws in this country. When the RCMP illegally opened mail, the government passed a law to make that act legal. That is what it just did in the freedom of information legislation. When the postal workers went out on a legal strike, the government passed a law to make it illegal. Those bills were the forerunners of this bill. But this bill is much broader.
In the same budget-not in this bill but it is part of the package-the government is raising the income tax of almost every Canadian through partial deindexing. It is lowering the real pension, the actual spending power of the pensioner. According to the government's own projections of inflation, the actual spending power will be lower. There is no reason to think that the government has overestimated inflation because in the past the government has always underestimated it. There will be a real drop in the value of the pension through partial deindexation.
There is the signal to all employers in Canada that this government now despises the principle of collective bargaining. In fact, it despises the principle of a contract. It is prepared to dishonour its contracts whenever it chooses. The government has openly advocated that the private employers of Canada should follow the government's lead in this dishonourable action and follow the government's lead in treating employees as second-class citizens in Canada.
On the other hand, there are giveaways to the wealthy through new schemes for indexing investment or investment income. As has been pointed out before, the principle of this
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
government is that if workers are to work harder it must give them less money; but for investors to work harder it must give them more money. This is how the government has corrupted the income tax system of this land in the same budget. This is in addition to all the tax gifts that were given to the same wealthy people in the November budget and by the concessions made since the November budget to the insurance companies and others in that field who appealed to the government about what I presume was their poverty and the difficulty of living on $100,000 a year. What this budget does is increase the revenue and power of that small group of people whose principal concern is to export Canada, primarily our raw materials, as fast as possible in order to get the quick bucks before the whole world economy collapses.
The budget supports the people who make their living by the revenues of the war industry, directly from the increased Canadian defence budget and indirectly by supplying materials to the much increased American war budget. It cuts the standard of living of working people directly. As well, it signals all power to the investor and employer class.
Why does the Minister of Finance do this? His stated reason is very simple, simplistic and false. For example, on July 5 in answer to the hon. member for Hamilton Mountain (Mr. Deans) he said, as reported on page 18983 of Hansard:
That is the logic of the budget statement, if all income demands-and I am putting the emphasis on all-
He did not do that before but he did it here because he realized he was talking to a union supporter.
-were reduced to 6 per cent, then price increases would drop to 6 per cent. That would be the inevitable result-
That is just pure hogwash. I do not think the Minister of Finance believes for a moment what he said. It is so nonsensical.
It is the same old hoary theory that the party opposite and the party to the right, when they have had their chance, have used since World War II. In spite of the social contract that was made at the end of the war, they have been chiselling away at it year by year with this same old hoary theory.
It used to be called the trickle down theory where you pour some in at the top and the people at the top get some, the people in the middle get some and the people at the bottom get some which makes everyone happy. The only thing that the sleight-of-hand people do not tell us about this trickle down theory is where the money comes from that is poured into the top. Of course, they got it from the taxpayers, who are primarily the low and middle-income people who cannot afford to hire accountants and lawyers to help them not pay any taxes at all. What this trickle down theory really says is that those lucky people at the botton, if they live long enough, may be able to get back some of what was taken away from them.
Of course, this is the same principle which is being followed here in Ontario by the Tory government. This is why that government has decided to bail out their friends, the private investors, by putting harsh new sales taxes on all these necessities needed by the people of Ontario. The only problem is that
