the trickle down theory does not work. It is catching up with them. As was pointed out last night, we now have approximately $135 billion of foreign debt which involves huge repayments that are becoming even larger each year. These repayments are laid on the working people of Canada.
Some have made rather mocking remarks about the foreign debt of Poland, suggesting that their foreign debt puts the Polish government in a crisis. Poland, with a much larger population than Canada, has a smaller foreign debt than Canada.
I think it is probably a fact that the decisions of those members in the front benches across the way are not really made in consultation with their backbenchers, let alone any serious debate with members on this side of the House. Decisions are certainly not made in any open, frank discussions with the people of Canada. The decisions made in the front benches, such as this one, I believe are made only in consultation with the international banking community, as was the case with the 1975 wage freeze.
We have a famous Canadian graduate who graduated to the United States as an economist. Mr. Galbraith recently seemed to have a sort of death bed repentance. He called this trickle down theory the horse and sparrow theory. He said that when he was a boy on a southern Ontario farm they talked about the horse and sparrow theory, which says that if you feed the horse enough oats some of them will fall on the ground for the sparrow too. When I read what Mr. Galbraith had written before, it was exactly that theory which he was preaching. He got rich by writing books which told people not to worry if the system is unjust and there is an unjust difference between the rich and the poor; we are all getting richer and we do not have to worry about the other person. He has now said that what he was talking about is nonsense. The only trouble with the horse and sparrow theory is that it does not work when you see that it is the sparrow which has to buy the oats for the horse.
Speaking of horses, in the Kensington area where I live we used to have a couple of junkmen or ragabonies, as some people called them. One old junkman in particular went through the streets with his horse, Betty, to pick up junk from people's yards to sell. He made a bare living that way. He could pay the rent, buy food for him and oats for Betty. As the prices went up he came to a crisis. He went out to the stable and said, "I am sorry, Betty, we have to tighten our belts". He gave Betty a few less oats each day until finally, on a Tuesday morning, he gave his horse no oats at all. He was a little slower on his rounds that day. The next day, Wednesday, he went to the stable and the horse lay dead on the floor. The junkman said: "Look at that ungrateful beast. Just when I taught her to live on nothing, she goes and dies on me!" I expect that that junkman voted Liberal. It is within living memory when people thought that Spadina was a safe Liberal riding. Maybe the horse voted Liberal also because we can remember when horses used to be on the payroll here, so why not on the voters' list?
From what 1 have seen, I do not believe that the people of Spadina or the people in the rest of Canada are as docile and willing to lie down and die as that horse. They will defend
themselves. They are saying that they do not like and will not accept a system which makes them the guinea pigs for an experiment that has already been proven false.
Why will they not accept it? First, they are the ones who have to carry the misery. They can see that it is not being carried by those who impose it on them. I have an unsolicited letter from a senior citizen in the city of Winnipeg. I used to live there, but that is not how the letter happened to come to me. He wrote, referring to the budget:
Please vote against the current "Budget" proposal which would limit to 6 per cent and 5 per cent respectively the increase in superannuation payments for the next two years.
I ask you to vote against this because while I was employed in the Federal Public Service, I paid the premiums required for insurance against "erosion of pensions' purchasing power".
In other words, he paid into the pension plan. Some of us are aware of the point he is making and agree with his letter. Others, though, especially those across the way, would rather the letters all went into the waste basket and were forgotten because they have a bad conscience for having cheated people out of the pensions for which they paid.
There are other workers in the Kensington area. Those making a living by hard work include construction workers, cleaners working for the minimum wage in the downtown buildings and the banks, the banks that made $1.5 billion in profits last year at the expense of low-wage workers, and viciously attack them when they try to organize unions. There are clerks working in places like Simpsons, which is laying off staff because customers are not coming in to buy since they do not have any money. There are maintenance workers who have been laid off, some of whom have been hunting for work for two years. In fact, in Kensington during the last decade or so a new industry has been developed: worm picking. At night the buses bring home the families consisting of fathers, mothers and children who have been out on the golf courses, or the lawns down in metro, picking worms. These are people who want to work and expect to work to maintain themselves, but who are not allowed to work because there are 1.5 million or two million unemployed in the country. These are people trying to make ends meet, although the cost of living is being pushed up by the deliberate, planned actions of the government.
Last month the price of food went up by 2.2 per cent, which was the largest monthly increase in two years. Apart from food, there are other big costs, such as shelter charges and gasoline prices. Just two weeks ago, the Prime Minister refused even to consider applying the guidelines to oil prices. There are increased costs for home heating and Bell telephone. Mortgage interest has increased 25.5 per cent over last year. Heating gas is up by 28.7 per cent over last year. Telephone service is up by 21.2 per cent and the company wants more in the next few months. The government will give it more. The government will stall and say: "Let the commission look into it and then we will consider it". By the time the government has
July 14, 1982

considered it, the company will be back for still another increase and it will also get that one from the government.
The government has created the very inflation that it said it is trying to fight. It has pushed prices up. It has not merely permitted them to rise, but has deliberately pushed them up for the last seven years through the interest policy of Governor Bouey. Therefore, the government blames the workers of Canada whose wages are 11 per cent lower than those in the United States, a land where the interest rates are also lower. The government blames workers in Canada for the government's decision to raise interest rates and all the other government administered charges.
We have seen an illustration of what was done to make the tax system more unequal; but now look at the deindexation of old age security. Under the indexed system, a person would have received $3,135.90 in 1983, but under the deindexed system it will be only $3,058.62, an absolute cut of $77.28. The next year, 1984, the cut will be $218.25, and so on, growing from year to year. Even if indexing were restored, it would be restored on that lower basis.
Women are especially restricted. At a time when there are huge changes coming in office machinery or procedures, women who follow the government's example, especially those in the government, are to be prevented from bargaining to protect either their jobs or their wages. Although only 39.6 per cent of total employees in the public sector are women, they make up 81.6 per cent of the support staff, the low-paid employees. When it comes to being laid off, these women, who equal 39.6 per cent of the employees, account for 54 per cent of those laid off.
What the working people of Canada understand is that the final pay-off of this system which makes them second-class citizens, blaming them for an inflation created by the government to the benefit of their employers, blaming them for being employees, is that the system will not even achieve the stated goal of cutting inflation. The 1975-78 wage freeze or, as the government likes to dress it up, "wage and price freeze", was a fraud and a failure for its stated goal of reducing inflation. It was a fraud because at the time it was introduced both prices and wages were already declining. In other words, prices and wages were coming down and the government decided to make it look as though it had done something by jumping on the bandwagon.
According to the budget figures put forward by the minister in November, wages in 1974 had gone up by 15.2 per cent, but in 1975 wage increases were down to 14.5 per cent. From there on, wage increases were 13.3 per cent, 8.3 per cent, 5.6 per cent and so on, on the way down, when the government put on a freeze. Likewise, prices were on the way down. They were 10.9 per cent the year before, 10.8 per cent when the government started its freeze and they dropped to 7.5 per cent. However, unlike wages, they did not keep going down. In 1977, while wages continued to go down, prices started coming up to 8 per cent. The next year, they were 8.9 per cent. In other words, while wage increases dropped from 14.5 per cent
Public Sector Compensation Restraint Act
to 5.6 per cent, the price rise dropped only from 10.8 per cent to 8.9 per cent. In other words, it was very successful in cutting wages and increasing profits. As the government has admitted in the study it did a year and a half ago, it was a failure in lowering prices. It was a fraud and a failure.
It is very interesting that at that time the Governor of the Bank of Canada more or less admitted that that was what was going on. At that time, in his annual report he said:
-through a sharp and immediate reduction of the growth rate of the money supply ... inflation would readily come to an end.
The trouble with this prescription is not with the medicine but with the dosage, which would be so great that the patient would suffer excessively while it was working. It would sharply curtail the growth of spending on goods and services-
He spoke as though he did not want this to occur, but in fact all his predictions occurred. He said:
It would sharply curtail the growth of spending on goods and services ... result in extremely weak markets, widespread bankruptcies and soaring unemployment.
Boy, do we ever have weak markets! He spoke as though he did not want to do this, but that is exactly what he did. At the time he spoke, unemployment was 6.9 per cent. Now, thanks to Bouey, it is 10.9 per cent and rising. At that time inflation was 9.5 per cent. Now it is 11.8 per cent. The bank rate was 9 per cent and it is now over 16 per cent. At that time there were 246 business bankruptcies per month. The figure is now over 900 per month. Consumer bankruptcies totalled 8,335 and have now nearly doubled to more than 14,000. In other words, the evil result that Mr. Bouey said he would like to avoid is exactly the result he has achieved with his systematic increase in interest rates.
The wage freeze of 1975-76 was a fraud and a failure. This one is a fraud and will be a failure. The people of Spadina and the rest of Canada will not accept this. They will not accept this attack on the wages, bargaining rights, pensions and income tax exemptions of the ordinary working people of Spadina and Canada. They will not accept government-made inflation of prices and the deliberately increased unemployment brought on by this government.
These people understand what the government meant a year and half ago when it said it could not bring in a wage freeze unless it could be made to be seen that there was some kind of emergency. They understand the government has created the sense or appearance of an emergency, or even a real emergency, to provide the excuse for bringing in the wage freeze.
These people understand that the government regularly defends the profits of the big corporations. 1 am not talking about the small businessmen, the merchants and manufacturers of Spadina. The government is wiping those out at a great rate. I am talking about the large corporations such as the oil companies and the banks.
The people of Spadina, Toronto and Canada understand that the government is the defender of those corporations. They are the first-class citizens even if they are not Canadians. Even if they do not live in Canada, they are the first-class

citizens here. The Minister of Finance said that everyone who is an employee is a second-class citizen and is condemned to be blamed for the inflation and unemployment which this government has created.
Some members opposite suggest it is not good enough merely to point out that their plan is a fraud and will fail, that some alternative ought to be offered. I remind them that the leader of our party, the hon. member for Oshawa (Mr. Broad-bent), has repeatedly put forward alternatives. I will touch on some of them.
The chief alternative that we ask for is a policy to replace imports so that we can restore our manufacturing industry and reduce our deficit in imported goods. We must replace imports of transportation machinery, not just automobiles but transportation, mining, forest and farm machinery, all those things we now import and which are increasing the deficit in this country. We must start to produce these items again in Canada. We should follow the lead of some other countries and impose restraints on the multinational corporations, telling them that if they want a slice of the Canadian market, they have to produce in Canada accordingly and provide jobs so that people can buy those products. They have to create jobs here of equal value to what they want to import into Canada.
We have suggested that investment be put into manufacturing rather than handouts to the poor, starving oil barons and the banks in the form of interest rates deliberately kept high. Public investment should be directed away from megaprojects and into manufacturing in order to provide employment for Canadians where they are, in the cities, with the skills they have and have shown.
There are four other points I wish to list. We must compel the banks to lower interest rates to 1 per cent above the inflation rate. We must be ready to impose foreign exchange controls to prevent investors from shipping abroad the capital produced by Canadian labour. If that has to be done by public control, or even expropriation of the banks as other countries have done, so be it.
Immediately we have to boost the affordable housing industry, not the luxury housing which the minister likes so much, with $500 million of investment to spark 50,000 new units and 100,000 new jobs. We have to boost farming with price stabilization and forestry and fisheries with programs for reforestation and regeneration of those resources.
We must give them an immediate shot in the arm once we have protected the Canadian economy from being raped by foreign investors. Then it would be appropriate to cut taxes for low and middle-income people and to cut the planned increases in oil prices in order to stimulate consumer buying. That would release about $4 billion, $2 billion from each. We should stimulate consumer buying and get our manufacturing industry going again, which now operates at about two-thirds capacity.
This is what should be done instead of this class legislation which will not work. It is being rejected by the Canadian
people. It cries out for a completely new social contract. This Liberal government with Tory backing has ripped up the social contract made with the working people of Canada in 1945. A new contract is needed.

Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), a success and show that in an area where at certain times of the year the unemployment rate is as much as 60 per cent, it is possible to reduce unemployment and improve conditions so that people can go on living there, to co-operate with the federal government and to obtain funds earmarked for this purpose. I wish to thank the Leader of the Opposition, Mr. Speaker, I may point out, however, that perhaps his advisers forgot to mention that, last year, the federal government injected $10 million into the local economy for the construction of wharves alone, and this year, in my own constituency, the federal government injected $3 million, and the fishermen from this part of Quebec and Canada are very pleased with the federal government's participation.
It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that the bill under consideration this afternoon demands the involvement and co-operation of all Canadians. When wage increases are frozen at 6 and 5 per

cent for the next two years, obviously no one is going to be too pleased. On the other hand, if we look at the economic situation throughout the country, we must set aside our personal interests and concentrate on the interests of the entire country. In his budget speech, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) said, and I quote:
1 will ask Canadians to participate in a strategy to make Canada a tougher, more resilient society. The way out of the recession is to bring down inflation and increase productivity. We must all share the burden and responsibility.
The government will take a leading role in this strategy.
I believe that, by this appeal, the Minister of Finance wanted to go beyond any political partisanship, any personal interest of individual Canadians. He was making a general appeal so that every one of us would put aside our personal ambitions or ideas to make a determined attack on the major problem now facing us, namely inflation. It is obvious that all of us, the government, the unions and business, must make every effort to reduce inflation throughout the country. Everyone must do his share. Obviously, the federal government had to show leadership in this area. For such a program to be successful, we must call on the generosity of everyone. The process which we began in the budget speech cannot succeed if every Canadian in every region of the country does not feel involved in the present debate.
I must say, Mr. Speaker, that we have already had examples throughout the country to show that there is some solidarity among Canadians and that some people are willing to share with others and be generous.
Let me just say, Mr. Speaker, that the experience of our own department of Employment and Immigration has shown for eight to ten months already that workers throughout the country can share with their fellow citizens. When we introduced the word-sharing program, we were appealing to the generosity of Canadian workers. If over 3,000 work-sharing agreements have now been signed in Canada, which agreements have preserved 115,000 jobs and allowed 52,000 workers to continue working in the same plants, it is precisely because other workers in these same plants were willing to reduce their wages and share with others who would otherwise have been laid-off. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that if these workers had not agreed to the work-sharing plan, if they had not shown this generosity in key industries in certain areas, these industries would have had to shut down and we would have had unemployment and jobless rates of 50, 60, 80 and even 90 per cent. We have here a striking example, Mr. Speaker, of the fact that Canadians are capable and willing to co-operate with each other in dealing with the major problem of the day- inflation.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, following the budget speech, the opposition reacted quite ruthlessly in some areas, but that was to be expected, because, whenever the government takes action or announces measures, it has been customary for the opposition, the media and all opposition groups in the country to

criticize the government in power. However, as people started to look at the budget and realized what was involved and looked at the economic situation throughout the country, opposition to the budget gradually faded. In a number of meetings held by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance with major groups in this country and in meetings held by other ministers with members on this side of the House, to explain the budget measures in greater detail, it became clear to many Canadians that the measures we were proposing were beneficial to the Canadian people. When the president of the Canadian Labour Congress came out of his meeting with the Prime Minister, some of our opposition friends did not particularly like his comments, but 1 think the president and some of his colleagues have understood that the serious situation we are experiencing today is the concern of all Canadians, that it is not just a problem to be solved not only by the Canadian government but also by the unions, workers, business, and all Canadians in this country.
Mr. Speaker, when we hear criticism of Bill C-124 and when people argue that we are going to gag the unions, that the right of strike will be more or less abolished throughout the public service, I would like to point out that we are now at the second reading stage. Negotiations and discussions can continue, and the Prime Minister said very clearly that all good suggestions, and I insist on the word good, will be given serious consideration by the government.
Obviously, we are not going to close the door on negotiations, and the bill now before the House is limited in time, because it will apply for a period of two years. All unions and all Canadians involved throughout the country will have an opportunity to express their views, to modify certain decisions and bring about changes in the state of the economy, during and beyond those two years.
Mr. Speaker, we must not forget that many Canadian industries have had to shut down because of the present economic crisis. If the measures we are proposing are successful in bringing down inflation, many industries will be able to remain active and many workers will be able to continue to work in these industries, which will prove beneficial to all Canadians. Mr. Speaker, it is important that we understand the measures this government wishes to introduce in the fight against inflation. Understandably, Canadians are not eager to see industries close down and people who have worked in these industries for twenty or thirty years lose their jobs, and often older people at that. No one likes to see these people lose their jobs.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?
